item.title: What Can Be Computed with Indefinite Causal Structure?
item.description: Can quantum computation become more powerful when operations do not need to follow a definite causal order? We study this question in the process matrix formalism of Oreshkov et al. (Nature Communications, 2012), which allows quantum operations to be connected without a fixed global order. In the computational model, a quantum circuit succinctly describes a process matrix, and the algorithm is given access to its generated channel, with computational cost measured by the size of the generating circuit. We give polynomial-time algorithms in two settings. First, general process matrix computation suffices to solve every problem in $\textbf{NP}$. The valid processes used by our algorithm satisfy the purification postulate of Araújo et al. (Quantum, 2017), and their generated channels are unitary, although their generating circuits are not. Second, requiring the process matrices themselves to be pure, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for unique-sink orientation, a general problem capturing several longstanding computational problems in optimization. Our unitary generators are constructed explicitly and efficiently. Assuming that unique-sink orientation has no quantum polynomial-time algorithm, our result shows that indefinite causal order can provide computational power beyond $\textbf{BQP}$ within the process matrix formalism, even while preserving unitarity.

item.title: Cubic lower bounds for the permanent in odd characteristic, for Pfaffian representations, and for polynomial entries
item.description: The determinantal complexity of a polynomial is the order of the smallest matrix whose entries are polynomials of degree at most one and whose determinant equals the polynomial. A lower bound for the permanent in this measure is the algebraic form of the question whether the permanent is harder to compute than the determinant. Over the complex numbers, the best known lower bound grows cubically in the size of the permanent. It holds even when the permanent only has to be a limit of such determinants. I prove that the cubic lower bound holds over every algebraically closed field of odd characteristic $p$, with a constant that depends on $p$. Hence the cubic bound does not depend on characteristic zero. I also prove the bound for Pfaffians, which are square roots of determinants of skew symmetric matrices. Lower bounds for Pfaffians imply the same bounds for determinants. Further, I prove the bound, divided by $a$, for matrices whose entries are polynomials of degree at most $a$. All three results come from one lower bound for smooth hypersurfaces. I prove it in every characteristic by counting intersection points together with their multiplicities.

item.title: Random ($\log{n}$)-CNF Formulas Are Hard for Depth-$2$ Frege with Modular Gates
item.description: We prove that, with high probability, refuting a random $k$-CNF formula on $n$ variables with ${M = n2^{k}}$ clauses for $ω_n(1) \leq k \leq O(\log{n})$ requires polynomial calculus degree at least ${n/2-O(n/\sqrt{k})}$ over every field. Through Pang's recent tradeoff between $\mathsf{AC}^0[p]$-Frege size and polynomial calculus degree [Pang 2026, arXiv:2610.00837v2], this implies a size lower bound of $\exp(Ω_p(\sqrt{k} \log{n}))$ for depth-$2$ $\mathsf{AC}^0[p]$-Frege. In this range of $k$, the bound is superpolynomial in $M$ while $M \leq \mathrm{poly}(n)$. We also prove a nearly matching degree upper bound of $n/2-n\ln(k)/{2k} +O(n/k)$, which shows that other formula families are needed to obtain lower bounds for full $\mathsf{AC}^0[p]$-Frege through Pang's tradeoff.

item.title: Retrieval Sequencing in a Compact Storage System with Side Access
item.description: In a compact storage system with side access, bins are arranged in adjacent vertical stacks. In each retrieval cycle, bins blocking access are lifted to create a temporary tunnel through which a robot extracts one requested bin from the side. The lifted bins are then lowered again, and the energy expenditure of the cycle equals the number of lifted bins. Given a pick list known in advance, we seek a retrieval order that minimizes total energy expenditure. For every number of stacks, we prove that the total energy separates into an instance constant and a pairwise penalty, and that every energy-optimal order is laminar within each stack. For two stacks, we prove that the retrieval sequencing problem is solvable in polynomial time. For three stacks, we give an exact polynomial-time reduction to a merge problem and characterize which merge-problem instances arise from the storage model. We define a recursive class of retrieval orders and construct a polynomial-time dynamic program that minimizes energy expenditure over this class. Finally, we quantify the additional energy savings from batching, which allows several requested bins to be retrieved in one cycle.

item.title: One Polynomial Field for Every Euler Step and the Flow: Polynomial Dynamics for P and PSPACE
item.description: We construct, for each deterministic Turing machine that halts on all inputs, one polynomial vector field with rational coefficients that performs the same logical computation at unit Euler step, at every smaller or variable step in $(0,1]$ with divergent sum, and along the flow. This unifies discrete-time and continuous-time computation by polynomial dynamics, which earlier characterizations treated separately. For a machine making $T$ transitions in space $H$, a logical scale $h=2^{-s}$ with $s=O(H)$ suffices, with physical time $O(s(T+s))$, drift disturbances up to $h^{2K}$ for a fixed exponent $K$, and $2Ks+3$ fractional bits at unit step. On a fixed compact domain, polynomial time and robust eventual decision characterize P and PSPACE, respectively, with polynomial scale thresholds and no supplied stabilization horizon in the space case. Without sign, floor or conditional primitives, margin amplification at bounded speed, overlapping polynomial gates and interval-product estimates give the common realization, from which we derive shared logical traces, fixed-field PSPACE-complete prediction and a robust safety family with polynomial certificates common to all Euler steps and the flow.

item.title: Mathematics and Efficiency of Song's CVP Hardness Reduction
item.description: Song (2026) proves that, for every fixed $0<ε<1$, the closest codeword problem (CCP) for binary linear codes under Hamming distance is NP-hard to approximate within $N^{1-ε}$, where $N$ is the code length, under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions. The code-to-lattice construction gives hardness within $N^{1/2-ε/2}$ for Euclidean CVP, with the same $N$ aslattice rank. This reaches every fixed Euclidean hardness exponent below one half. Aharonov and Regev (2005), with the constant refined by Gao (2026), place GapCVP at factor $cN^{1/2}$ in $\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}$ for every fixed $c>2/(π\sqrt3)\approx0.3676$. NP-hardness at that scale would imply $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}$. This paper has two goals: to explain Song's theorem and its mathematics for graduate students, and to make the reduction more efficient. The reduction turns satisfiability into a system of quadratic equations and then into CCP for binary linear codes, and recovers assignments from recurrence relations of algebraic moments. We adapt the method to linear codes over any fixed finite field of characteristic $p$. A common recurrence for each block column gives a moment window $L=c_p(κ-1)+1$, where $c_p=\max\{2,p-1\}$ and $κ$ is the rank cutoff. Together with ordinary digit products and flexible sampling, this reduces interpolation degrees and output lengths. For CCP gap $N^{1-ε}$, our explicit schedule gives code length and lattice rank at most $n^{4/ε^2+O(1/ε)}$; Song's prescribed binary schedule gives $n^{8/ε^2+O(1/ε)}$. Here $n$ counts variables in a common quadratic system, equal to the number of original variables plus clauses for 3SAT. These are dimension bounds, not optimality claims or running-time exponents. The limiting hardness exponents remain Song's.

item.title: How Hard Is It to Compute Cover Time?
item.description: It is $\#\mathrm{P}\text{-hard}$. Even for connected simple undirected unweighted graphs, deciding whether an expected random-walk cover time is at most a given rational threshold is $\#\mathrm{P}\text{-hard}$ under polynomial-time Turing reductions, both from a specified starting vertex and when maximized over starting vertices. Both families have a universal vertex, called the hub, and diameter two. Deleting the hub leaves a planar bipartite graph, and every non-hub vertex has degree at most five. A shared construction encodes an Euler-tour count in rare covering walks. For specified starts, a number of fractional bits linear in the queried graph's vertex count suffices for recovery. For the maximum-start problem, a fixed cube attachment makes the maximizing starts known, and one interpolation of expected cover times recovers the count. Both reductions use polynomial-size graphs and polynomial-bit threshold queries. For general graphs, both comparison problems can be solved in polynomial time with access to an $\mathrm{NP}^{\mathrm{PP}}$ oracle.

item.title: Maxwell's equations are universal for sparse linear algebra
item.description: Optical and wave-based analog computing has re-emerged as a route to accelerating linear algebra, with metamaterials and photonic circuits shown to invert matrices and solve integral equations. However, it has remained unclear which problems such passive structures can represent, and at what cost, once encoding, precision, conditioning and readout are accounted for. Here, we show that every polynomially conditioned sparse linear system can be compiled into a three-dimensional dielectric -- a cavity filled with lossless, isotropic material of bounded permittivity -- whose time-harmonic response encodes its solution. For $m$ nonzero coefficients, the volume of the structure and the cost of writing it down and reading out the answer scale as $\tilde O(m^{3/2})$, coefficients require only $O(\log m)$ bits, and every field that approximately satisfies Maxwell's equations decodes to an approximate solution. We prove the construction for the continuum equations and give a computer-assisted version for the Yee discretization underlying finite-difference solvers. Read in reverse, it implies that electromagnetic simulation is, up to this overhead, as hard as general sparse linear algebra: a sufficiently fast general-purpose Maxwell solver would yield a faster sparse linear solver.

item.title: Local Quantum Fault Tolerance Without Expansion
item.description: We study fault-tolerant quantum computation using a fixed, local error-correction rule and a geometrically simple code: the cubical $(d,d')$-Toric code with $d',d-d'\geq 2$, including the 4D Toric code. Under sufficiently weak local-stochastic Pauli noise, our construction uses noiseless, bounded-depth classical processing per physical time step. Its correction cycle acts only on the current syndrome, has constant depth, and is repeated unchanged during idle logical computation; it requires neither multiscale decoder states nor scale-dependent communication delays. Our proof treats errors and syndromes as chains in a cubical complex, combining geometric shrinking under the sweep rule with a space--time explanation-tree argument inspired by Toom's theorem. It does not rely on expansion. We establish three results: 1.Explicit higher-dimensional sweep rule. We give a local algorithm for choosing sweep corrections on cubical $(d,d')$-Toric complexes, resolving the local-existence question of Kubica and Preskill. 2. Fault-tolerant computation. We prove a circuit-level threshold theorem for noisy sweep cycles interleaved with logical gates. In particular, the 4D Toric code admits a fixed, constant-depth syndrome-based correction cycle without a multiscale decoder or expansion-based encoding. We do not claim constant total-depth overhead. 3. Ideal decoding under local-stochastic noise. For an initial local-stochastic Pauli error of rate $p$ below threshold, $n^{d+1}$ noiseless sweep cycles recover the encoded state on a side-length-$n$ $(d,d')$-Toric code with probability at least $1-O(\operatorname{poly}(n))p^{Ω(n)}$, extending earlier guarantees for independent errors.

item.title: A Witnessing Duality for ReLU Network Depth
item.description: A depth lower bound for ReLU networks asserts that every shallower network errs on some input; we ask when a weak theory can prove such a bound so that an error can be computed. For the exact computation of $\max(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, recent work shows two hidden layers suffice with unrestricted rational weights. By contrast, Haase, Hertrich and Loho (ICLR 2023) proved that integer weights require depth logarithmic in $n$, and Averkov, Hojny and Merkert (ICLR 2025) extended the bound to nonbias weights whose denominators are powers of a fixed integer not divisible by a prime $q$. With integer weights the bound is sharp: the classical balanced construction has depth $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. For each fixed $q$ and depth cap $K$, we prove this known bound in $\mathbf{VTC}^0$, the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation, together with a refuter that is itself such a computation and whose correctness the theory proves. Given a network with at most $K$ hidden layers, nonbias weights whose reduced denominators avoid $q$, arbitrary rational biases and $n>q^K$ inputs, the refuter returns a rational input of polynomial length on which the network errs. The proof makes the obstruction finite: an iterated intersection product of piecewise-linear functions is divisible by $q$ for the network but not for the maximum, so one of finitely many test points exposes the error. By witnessing, provable refutation corresponds to a provably correct refuter, and provable existence of a certified network to a provably correct constructor. On the construction side, we introduce certificates that label each maximum gadget by the inputs it aggregates; with them the theory verifies the balanced construction, which meets the refuter at the sharp threshold $n\le2^K$, and a rational family of polynomial description length and depth $O(\log n/\log\log n)$ built from known depth-two blocks.

item.title: Ancilla-free randomized Toffoli gates and the T-count of Boolean oracles
item.description: In fault-tolerant Clifford+T circuits, a Boolean oracle costs T gates and extra qubits, and on four or more qubits every exact Toffoli gate needs an extra qubit. Gosset, Kothari and Zhang showed that sampling a fresh random circuit for each call makes the T-count of the Toffoli gate independent of its size, but a direct implementation of their sampler uses about one extra qubit per bit of precision. We show that computing the sampled parities in place, on the gate's own controls, removes every extra qubit once the gate is large enough: each random circuit then uses about 8 T gates per bit of precision and borrows only the gate's own idle inputs. This is one T gate more per circuit than the best measurement-free variant that keeps one clean ancilla. The same holds for exclusive-ors of indicators of affine subspaces, such as equality tests and checks of linear equations. For randomized circuits that do not measure, this is within a factor of eight of optimal up to an additive constant, even with extra qubits, and when each random circuit computes a Boolean function exactly, closing the factor asymptotically is equivalent to determining the leading constant in the T-count of exact multi-controlled Toffoli gates. Finally, the oracle of the indicator of a random set of fixed density needs exponentially many T gates at constant error, while that of an affine subspace of the same density needs a constant number, and extra qubits reduce the exponential cost only quadratically.

item.title: Separations between $\#\mathrm{BIS}$ and $\#\mathrm{IS}$
item.description: We give complexity-theoretic separations between $\#\mathrm{BIS}$ and $\#\mathrm{IS}$. Given a graph $G$, and a fugacity $λ>0$, the hard-core model is given by $Z_G(λ)=\sum_{I\in\mathcal I(G)}λ^{|I|}$, where $\mathcal I(G)$ denotes the independent sets of $G$. For $F\ge1$, an $F$-factor approximation to $Z_G(λ)$ is an estimate $\widehat Z$ satisfying $F^{-1}Z_G(λ)\le\widehat Z\le FZ_G(λ)$. Let $\mathcal G_Δ$ denote the class of $Δ$-regular graphs and $\mathcal G_{Δ,Δ}$ the class of $Δ$-regular bipartite graphs. We give two separation results. (1) There exist an integer $Δ\ge3$, a sufficiently large fugacity $λ$, and a constant $c>0$ so that the following hold: (a) For every $δ\in(0,1)$, deterministic $(1+δ)$-factor approximation on $\mathcal G_{Δ,Δ}$ is possible in time $\exp(cn)\operatorname{poly}(n,1/δ)$. (b) Under the Gap-Exponential Time Hypothesis, there exists no deterministic algorithm running in time $\exp(2cn)\operatorname{poly}(n)$ on $\mathcal G_Δ$ that gives an $\frac{11}{10}$-factor approximation. (2) For every fixed $Δ\ge3$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, for all sufficiently large fugacities $λ$, the following hold: (a) There exists an algorithm which outputs a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon)^n$-factor approximation to $Z_G(λ)$ on $\mathcal G_{Δ,Δ}$ in polynomial time. (b) Under the assumption $\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}$, there exists no deterministic polynomial-time algorithm on $\mathcal G_Δ$ that gives a $(1+\varepsilon)^n$-factor approximation. Both our algorithmic results follow from a new spanning-tree encoding of independent sets that enables an efficient representation of large independent sets.

item.title: Lower Bound for Region of Non-Distillable Magic States
item.description: Magic states are a leading proposal for realizing fault-tolerant and universal quantum computation. At the present moment, much of the theory of magic states is not understood. Even simple questions such as what single qubit states have magic remain open. In Campbell and Browne's seminal paper on bound magic states, they prove the existence of states outside of the stabilizer octahedron which cannot be used to achieve universal computation. In this paper we expand upon their proof and determine a lower-bound on this region.

item.title: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy
item.description: It is not known whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can verify arbitrary polynomial-time quantum computations with an efficient quantum honest prover without computational assumptions. We show that, relative to a classical oracle, such verification is possible for a language beyond the polynomial hierarchy that is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time. The protocol is public-coin, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4. To our knowledge, no language with such a proof system was previously proved to lie outside AM relative to an oracle. For every unbounded polynomial-time computable function, the oracle can be chosen so that the message count and the oracle query counts of the quantum algorithm, verifier, and honest prover are bounded by this function of the input length. The message count is optimal up to a constant factor, since for a suitable oracle every interactive proof system for the language uses at least a constant fraction of the messages of our protocol on infinitely many lengths, with a constant depending on its verifier. The language is a variant of recursive Fourier sampling in which code tables encode secrets that address data tables. The tables are evaluated recursively, and the oracle stores only the leaves. The quantum algorithm recovers every secret exactly, and the verifier checks the prover's secrets recursively against random code entries. The recursion restricts the input in a correlated way, as the same secret fixes the code bits and chooses the free coordinate, so Håstad's switching lemma does not apply. We prove a switching theorem for these restrictions, which may be of independent interest. For instances of sufficient height, no constant-depth circuit of size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ changes its output with probability above $2^{-Ω(n)}$ when the answer of a random instance is flipped by changing a single leaf.

item.title: Upper and Lower Bounds on the Complexity of Unit-Distance Graph Realization in $\mathbb{Z}^d$
item.description: It is known that the problem of recognizing the existence of a unit-distance realization in $\mathbb{Z}^d$ for a graph $G$ is NP-complete. Here, assuming ETH, we give a sub-exponential lower bound of $2^{Ω(\sqrt{n})}$ for this problem in $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and $2^{Ω(n^{2/3})}$ in $\mathbb{Z}^3$, and give an upper bound of $2^{O(n^{(d-1)/d} (\log n)^2)}$ for the time complexity with an explicit divide-and-conquer algorithm. This approach beats naive exhaustive search by a factor of $\tildeΩ(n^{1/d})$ in the exponent. For 2 and 3 dimensions, our upper and lower bounds match to within a logarithmic factor.

item.title: Computational complexity of the $H$-coloring problem in cubic graphs
item.description: If $G$ and $H$ are two cubic graphs, then an $H$-coloring of $G$ is a mapping $f: E(G)\rightarrow E(H)$, such that for every $v\in V(G)$ there is a vertex $x\in V(H)$, such that $f(\partial_G(v))=\partial_H(x)$. If $G$ admits an $H$-coloring then it is common to write $H\prec G$. In this paper, for a fixed connected cubic graph $H$, we consider a decision problem, which we call $H$-coloring. In this problem, on the input one is given a connected cubic graph $G$. The goal is to decide whether $H\prec G$. A conjecture by Hakobyan and the author states that $H$-coloring is polynomial time solvable, if $H$ does not admit a $P_{12}$-coloring. Here $P_{12}$ is the unique cubic graph obtained from the Petersen graph by expanding one of its vertices into a triangle. In this paper, we disprove this conjecture under $P\neq NP$, by showing that $S_6$-coloring is NP-complete. Here $S_6$ is the unique cubic graph on six vertices having exactly one bridge. Our second result is an algorithm that solves $H$-coloring problem in time $O^*(c^n)$, where $H$ is a simple connected cubic graph, $n$ is the number of vertices of the input cubic graph $G$ and $c=\sqrt{8}\approx 2.8284$.

item.title: Improved Quasi-Polynomial-Time Approximation for Maximum Independent Set
item.description: We give a deterministic quasi-polynomial-time algorithm for the maximum independent set problem. If an $N$-vertex graph contains an independent set of size $2^{-t}N$, where $t$ is an integer with $1\le t\le\sqrt{\log N}/12$, then our algorithm finds an independent set of size $2^t$ in time $N^{O(t)}$. This gives an approximation ratio of $N/2^{Ω(\sqrt{\log N})}$ in time $N^{O(\sqrt{\log N})}$, improving on the approximation ratio $N/2^{Ω((\log N)^{1/3})}$ obtained by Lovett [Lov26]. A limitation of this form of analysis follows from the integrality gaps of Tulsiani [Tul09]. These gaps imply that a universal guarantee of the form $\operatorname{Las}_{R(t)}(G)\ge2^{-t}N\Longrightarrowα(G)\ge2^t$, at $2^{o(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})}$ levels, cannot hold over a range extending beyond $t=O(\sqrt{\log N\log\log N})$. Thus, the exponent $1/2$ is the limit of this form of analysis, up to a factor of $\sqrt{\log\log N}$.

item.title: Linear Hashing Is Poissonesque
item.description: The Poisson approximation theorem states that when $m$ balls are tossed uniformly and randomly into $n$ bins, the distribution of the bin loads can sometimes be approximated by $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. We show that when the balls are tossed via a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map, the load distribution is still governed by this Poisson distribution, albeit in a (necessarily) weaker manner. This allows us to show that a random linear map behaves like a fully random map in the following ways: 1. $\textbf{Expected loads.}$ We show that the expected value of the $r$th largest bin is governed by the $r$th largest value among $n$ independent Poisson random variables of mean $m/n$. Specializing to the canonical setting of $m=n$ and $r=1$, our bounds show that the expected maximum load when $n$ balls are hashed into $n$ bins by a random $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear map is no more than the corresponding expectation for a fully random map $\textit{plus}$ $\frac{3}2 + o(1)$. Specializing to $m\gg n\log n$, we show that the expected max load is $(1+o(1))m/n$ in this regime. 2. $\textbf{Concentration.}$ When $m\gg n\log (1/ρ)$ balls are tossed into $n$ bins randomly, we expect with $0.99$ probability that $\textit{every}$ density-$ρ$ subset of bins will contain a $(1\pm o(1) )ρ$-fraction of the balls. We show that this remains the case if the $m$ balls are tossed using a random linear map, and our bound matches the $o(1)$-factor produced by the fully random case. This gives a stronger version of the Leftover Hash Lemma for linear maps. An implication of this is that all bins have load $m/n \pm O(\sqrt{(m/n)\log n})$ with probability $0.99$. We obtain these results by showing that the average of a log-potential on the bin loads is upper bounded by the cumulant generating function of a Poisson random variable of mean $m/n$.

item.title: Propositional formula minimization is $Σ_2^p$-complete under many-one reductions
item.description: The Minimum Equivalent Expression problem (MEE) asks, given a propositional formula $φ$ and an integer $k$, whether $φ$ is equivalent to a formula with at most $k$ occurrences of propositional variables. While the problem is clearly in $Σ_2^p$, its completeness under polynomial-time many-one reductions has remained open since at least 1979. Buchfuhrer and Umans showed in 2008 that it is $Σ_2^p$-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions. In this note, we present a proof discovered by GPT-Sol-6.1 which establishes that MEE is $Σ_2^p$-complete also under polynomial-time many-one reductions.

item.title: Unconditional Lower Bounds for the Fredman--Khachiyan Algorithms for Monotone Boolean Duality Testing
item.description: We prove unconditional lower bounds on the number of recursive calls made by the two algorithms of Fredman and Khachiyan (1996) for monotone Boolean duality testing, as a function of the explicit input size $N$. For Algorithm A we show a lower bound of $N^{Ω(\log N)}$ on the dual pairs $(\HH_k,\LL_k)$ obtained from the read-once family of Gurvich and Khachiyan. The proof lower-bounds the number of leaves of every binary decision tree computing the function by the modulus of its multilinear polynomial evaluated at a complex point of the unit circle. It therefore applies to every choice of branching variables and, more generally, to the class of two-child variable-restriction procedures whose terminal calls have polynomially bounded decision-tree complexity. On this family the number of calls is exactly $N^{Θ(\log N)}$. For Algorithm B, a symmetric specialization of the polynomial padding construction of Kobayashi, Kurita, and Wasa, with full polynomial blocks, yields at least $q^{(t-1)k-t(t-1)/2}$ calls, where $k=4t^2$ and $q=Θ(t^2)$; as a function of $N$ this is $N^{Ω(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ along an infinite family. In an appendix we show that applying the padding construction directly to Algorithm A gives $Ω(2^n)$ calls on a dual pair obtained from an unsatisfiable $n$-variable formula, which is only $N^{Ω(\sqrt{\log N/\log\log N})}$ in terms of the input size. No complexity-theoretic assumption is used. The proofs allow every branching-variable choice permitted by the respective algorithm. They concern the original recursive procedures, counting every invocation separately, without sharing calls or adding positive stopping tests.

item.title: Asymptotic Rank of Complete Graph Tensors
item.description: Graph tensors extend the matrix multiplication tensor by placing a two-party identity tensor on every edge of a graph and keeping one tensor leg at every vertex. We study the asymptotic rank of the tensor associated with the complete graph. For every integer $n\geq 2$, over the complex numbers, we prove \[ \left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor \leq \log_2\widetilde R\bigl(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n)\bigr) \leq \frac{n^2}{4}. \] The upper bound matches the maximum-cut lower bound for every even $n$ and differs from it by only $1/4$ for every odd $n$. In particular, the exponent per edge is below $2/3$ for every $n\geq5$, answering a question of Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam. Our proof extends the polynomial multiplication approach underlying OpenAI's bound $ω\leq9/4$. The main step separates any fixed number of shared tensor legs simultaneously, using only linearly many direct-sum copies in the number of blocks. This yields an entropy inequality for higher-order tensors. We apply it to the tensor for multiplying $n-1$ polynomials, whose rank is linear in the input length. Discrete concavity and a shifted tripling inequality then force a lower bound on a symmetrized spectral profile. Comparing this growth with polynomial interpolation gives the stated upper bound while preserving all $n$ tensor legs. We also prove an operational barrier for these higher-order polynomial constructions. For $n\geq3$, the specified formal reduction rules cannot certify an exponent below $n^2/4$ for $\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n)$, even after taking tensor powers and allowing subexponential overhead and common auxiliary factors. This extends the symmetric three-leg barrier of Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam and explains the remaining gap for odd complete graphs within this method.

item.title: A Borsuk-Ulam theorem for adaptive continuous measurements
item.description: We prove a Borsuk-Ulam theorem for adaptive measurements: if $2^n\le m$, then any $n$ adaptively chosen continuous functionals take identical values at two antipodal points of any sphere in $\mathbb{R}^m$. Consequently, at least $\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil$ adaptive continuous measurements are needed to learn the vectors of a ball in $\mathbb{R}^m$ with an error smaller than its radius, which matches the recently obtained upper bound up to one measurement. The bound extends to Bernstein widths in Banach spaces. The main idea of the proof was found by Claude Fable 5, an AI model developed by Anthropic, and we document the development in a last section.

item.title: Communication Complexity of Integer Matrix Singularity
item.description: Alice and Bob hold complementary halves of the columns of an $n\times n$ matrix of $k$-bit integers and decide whether it is singular over $\mathbb Q$. Up to constant-factor dimension growth, this partitioned problem is equivalent to additive singularity, where Alice and Bob hold $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$ of $k$-bit integers and test the singularity of $A+B$ over $\mathbb Q$. We prove a bounded-error quantum lower bound $Ω(\min\{n^{3/2}\sqrt{k\log n},n^2\log(nk)\})$ and a randomized upper bound $O(n^2\min\{k,\log(k+\log n)\})$. The bounds match at $Θ(n^2\log(nk))$ for $k\ge n\log n$. The lower bound holds even under the promise of rank $n-1$ versus $n$. Its proof combines an integer witness with a local digit encoding, while the upper-bound protocol lifts modular kernel relations using short messages. Bitwise sharing changes how the communication complexity depends on the entry bit length $k$. If Alice and Bob instead hold $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$ of $k$-bit integers and test whether their entrywise bitwise XOR $A\oplus B$ is singular over $\mathbb Q$, we prove a quantum lower bound $Ω(n^2k)$, matching the trivial upper bound. This lower bound holds even under the promise of rank $n-1$ versus $n$. Our proof uses a dense weighted equation and a signed Fourier witness whose exceptional dyadic frequencies can be removed at small variation cost.

item.title: On the complexity of Medvedev reducibility
item.description: The Medvedev lattice is a tool used to classify the complexity of effective closed sets. In this article, we are interested in the complexity of using this tool. In particular, we study the complexity of deciding whether two effective closed sets have the same degree, when one is fixed and the other is given as input. This problem is naturally~$Σ^0_3$, and among other results, we show that for all degrees except the maximal one, the problem reaches its maximal complexity. It turns out that the argument is not uniform and depends on the self-similarity of the fixed degree, a notion that we introduce in this article. The complexity of having maximal degree is particularly difficult to establish, but we obtain a lower bound that almost matches the upper bound. We also show that deciding whether an effective closed set has a degree incomparable with a fixed degree $d$ is $Π^0_3$-complete whenever $\mathbf{0}_s <_s d <_s \mathbf{1}_s$.

item.title: Deterministic Root-Finding over Finite Fields with Elliptic Curves
item.description: Finding the roots of a polynomial over a finite field $\mathbb F_q$ in deterministic polynomial time is a long-standing open problem. Classical deterministic methods work in the multiplicative group $\mathbb F_q^\times$ and are efficient only when $q-1$ is smooth, which is rarely the case. We propose a method that replaces $\mathbb F_q^\times$ by the groups of rational points of an elliptic curve $E$ and of its quadratic twist $\widetilde E$. The computation splits into an offline phase, which depends only on $\mathbb F_q$ and outputs a short \emph{elliptic preprocessing datum} $\mathcal D$, and an online phase, which processes the input polynomial. Writing $Ξ(\mathcal D)$ for the largest prime factor of $\lvert E(\mathbb F_q)\rvert\cdot\lvert\widetilde E(\mathbb F_q)\rvert$, the online phase is deterministic and finds the roots of any $f\in\mathbb F_q[X]$ of degree $n$ within $\widetilde O(Ξ(\mathcal D)^2\,n\log^2 q+n^ω\log q+n\log^3 q)$ operations in $\mathbb F_q$. A precursor of our method is an algorithm by Rónyai, which recovers the roots through Galois computations over number fields, relies on GRH, and comes with a polynomial bound of unspecified degree; in contrast, our online phase works entirely over $\mathbb F_q$ and is unconditional. Moreover, $\mathcal D$ can be certified deterministically and unconditionally in time polynomial in $\log q$ and $Ξ(\mathcal D)$. We conjecture that every $\mathbb F_q$ of large enough characteristic admits a datum with $Ξ(\mathcal D)\leq(\log q)^{O(1)}$, and support this with a heuristic and with experiments. Constructing such a datum in polynomial time remains open.

item.title: Settling Nondeterministic Communication Complexity of Graph Connectivity
item.description: Determining the communication complexity of graph connectivity has been one of the longest standing open problems in communication complexity since the seminal work of Babai, Frankl, and Simon [FOCS'86]. A simple protocol transmits a spanning forest using $O(N\log N)$ communication on $N$-vertex graphs. While this was shown optimal for deterministic protocols by Hajnal, Maass, and Turán [STOC'88], the optimal nondeterministic and randomized complexities have remained unresolved for decades. We settle the nondeterministic communication complexity of graph connectivity by proving an optimal $Ω(N\log N)$ lower bound. The best prior bound was $Ω(N\log\log N)$ due to Raz and Spieker [Combinatorica'95]. Our bound is shown by upper bounding the maximum size of $1$-monochromatic rectangles. Generalizing our techniques to weighted, almost $1$-monochromatic rectangles yields an $Ω(N \cdot \log(\min(1/\varepsilon,N)))$ lower bound for randomized protocols with error probability $\varepsilon$. In particular, this bound is optimal for any polynomially small $\varepsilon$. For constant error probability, we also prove that any $r$-round protocol requires $Ω(N/r \cdot \log N)$ communication, which is optimal for every constant $r$. Previously, optimal $Ω(N\log N)$ lower bounds for graph connectivity were known only for $1$-round [Sun, Woodruff; APPROX/RANDOM'15] and $2$-round protocols [Radhakrishnan, Reddy, Venkat; ITCS'26]. Our proof introduces a new communication problem which can be viewed as a composition of inner product and pointer chasing problems. Our lower bounds can be extended to other fundamental graph properties, and also imply optimality of known query and streaming algorithms for related problems.

item.title: On the Propeller Conjecture
item.description: We simplify and improve OpenAI's proof of the propeller conjecture of Khot and Naor from 2008: the sum of the squared lengths of the Gaussian moments of any partition of Euclidean space is at most $9/(8π)$. We show equality only occurs for three 120 degree sectors in the plane (up to symmetries, measure zero changes, and taking orthogonal cross products with Euclidean space). We also remove computer assistance from the three-dimensional case of the conjecture, which previously used an epsilon net traversal.

item.title: No Perfect Randomized Composition
item.description: Does computing a composition of total Boolean functions require the product of the randomized query complexities of its factors? We give a negative answer. There are families of total functions $f,g$ such that $R(f\circ g) =Θ\!\left(\frac1{\log R(g)}\right)R(f)R(g)$ This result requires first separating linearized query complexity $\LR$, as well as noisy randomized query complexity $noisyR$, from standard randomized query complexity $R$. Both constructions essentially come from totalizing existing partial function separations, albeit via different techniques. By adapting these techniques, we also construct total functions separating every adjacent pair in the chain from sabotage $RS$, max-conflict $\barχ$, and linearised query complexity $LR$. We show that AND-of-ORs separates conflict $χ$ from max-conflict $\barχ$ complexity and makes conflict and sabotage incomparable. Finally, randomized complexity can be smaller than its composition limit $R^*$ by the maximal factor $Θ(\log R)$. The total--total composition separation is also formalized in Lean.

item.title: Near-Quadratic Time Multivariate Polynomial Interpolation
item.description: Let $\F$ be a finite field. Given $N$ distinct points $\bmα_1,\ldots,\bmα_N \in \F^m$ and associated values $β_1,\ldots,β_N \in \F$, we study the problem of computing an $m$-variate polynomial $f(\vy) \in \F[\vy]$ of individual degree less than $d$, with $d^m \ge N$, that satisfies $f(\bmα_i)=β_i$ for all $i\in[N]$, whenever such an $f$ exists. This is known as the\textit{ multivariate polynomial interpolation} problem. In this work, given $N=d^m$, we present a deterministic algorithm for multivariate polynomial interpolation over an arbitrary finite field $\F$ that runs in near-quadratic time $N^{2+o(1)}\poly(m,d,\log|\F|)$, assuming $d$ is $ω(1)$. This bound holds whenever the associated \emph{multivariate Vandermonde} matrix is nonsingular, has constant co-rank, or admits some special structure. In the general case, we give a randomized Las Vegas algorithm attaining the same near-quadratic running time, provided the finite field is sufficiently large and $d$ grows similar to the previous case. Unlike other multivariate interpolation strategies, we do not assume black-box access to the polynomial. In particular, we are not permitted to query arbitrary input points to obtain their evaluations. Our interpolation result follows by combining Wiedemann's classical approach~\cite{w86} for solving sparse linear systems with known bounds for fast \emph{multivariate multipoint evaluation} over finite fields~\cite{umans08, KU11, BGKM23, BGGKU24}. Specifically, our deterministic interpolation strategy relies on a deterministic variant of Wiedemann's approach, which is more commonly used in the randomized setting.

item.title: Two-colour crossing minimization in complete geometric graphs is NP-hard
item.description: Given a fixed straight-line drawing of a complete graph, we seek a two-colouring of its edges that minimizes the number of monochromatic crossing pairs. We prove that the threshold decision problem is NP-complete, even when the vertices are in general position and have integer coordinates of polynomial binary length. Thus exact minimization is NP-hard, answering the complexity question posed at the Crossing Number Workshop in 2019. The reduction is from MaxCut on permutation graphs. Its main difficulty is to control the edges required by completeness, whose colours must remain free. We construct a large comparison grid with two stable colour phases and use additional points to assign costs to the edges that encode the source graph. A geometric separation eliminates one large class of unwanted crossings. The costs of all remaining edges are included in a computable baseline and bounded errors, with each unit of the source objective amplified beyond the total error. The construction is deterministic and has polynomial size and coordinate bit length.

item.title: Tight Bounds on the Randomized Communication Complexity of Vector-in-Subspace
item.description: We prove that the randomized communication complexity of Vector-in-Subspace in $\mathbb R^n$ with error at most $1/3$ is $Θ(\sqrt n)$. Alice holds a unit vector $u$ and Bob holds an $n/2$-dimensional subspace $H$; they must distinguish $u\in H$ from $u\in H^\perp$. An exact one-way quantum protocol uses $O(\log n)$ qubits, making the problem a geometric example of an exponential quantum advantage over interactive classical communication. Our lower bound matches Raz's $O(\sqrt n)$ upper bound, improves the $Ω(n^{1/3})$ lower bound of Klartag and Regev, and removes the total-rank restriction in Grupel's $Ω(\sqrt n)$ result. The proof establishes a Gaussian moment bound over complete rectangle partitions. A complex Gaussian representation yields a vanishing even moment whose cancellation is preserved when averaging over the partition. We control the signed conditional moments around a real center by decomposing conditional Gaussian measures into fixed coordinates and sub-Gaussian components. Combining this estimate with spherical harmonic analysis gives the communication lower bound.

item.title: Dissipation Bounds and Hardness in Globally Asymptotically Stable Quadratic Systems
item.description: We study worst-case finite-time energy dissipation in quadratic systems with proved global asymptotic stability (GAS). Estimating the maximum retained energy fraction to any fixed positive additive error below $1/2$ is NP-hard, even when the input includes a strict quartic Lyapunov function and proof of strictness, both constructed in polynomial time. NP denotes nondeterministic polynomial time. For a partially damped family, the unit-sphere minimum norm of the coupling map equals the structured coefficient distance to loss of GAS. Positive distances at most $1/2$ give two-sided inverse-square halving-time bounds with explicit coefficient factors. Polynomial-factor approximation of the least dissipated fraction, halving time or coefficient distance is NP-hard. Additive hardness persists throughout an explicit coefficient neighborhood and under direct damping with exponential stability, a strict quadratic Lyapunov function and a Hurwitz Jacobian. Unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, where P denotes deterministic polynomial time, no polynomial-time algorithm attains these guarantees on all inputs.

item.title: Amplified Pruning and Path Selectors for Deterministic Radio Gossiping
item.description: We study deterministic gossiping in unknown strongly connected directed radio networks with $n$ vertices, $m$ arcs, and distinct identifiers in $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, where $N=n^{\mathcal O(1)}$. Messages are unrestricted; collision detection is unavailable. Our protocol combines amplified reception certificates, adaptive pruning, and permutation selectors. Each pruning iteration costs $\mathcal O(n\log^2n\log\log n)$ rounds. A two-step quadratic contraction limits each receiver and each class of identical closed in-neighborhoods to $\mathcal O(\log\log n)$ qualifying selections. Under an explicit degree-concentration condition, our protocol takes $\mathcal O(m\log^2n(\log\log n)^2)$ rounds. For directed regular graphs with common in- and out-degree $Δ$, our strategy achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n\sqrtΔ,n^2/Δ\})$, extending the identifier range of Wu and Chrobak and improving their high-degree bound. At completion entry, let $a\ge1$ count original sources not yet credited as globally disseminated. Permutation selectors reduce our balanced completion budget by a factor of $\log^{2/3}(a+1)$ relative to interleaved path selectors. Our geometric protocol attains $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(k^2+nτ+\min\{u^2,(nu)^{2/3}\})$ for an original path cover of scale $k$, weight $τ$, and $u$ exceptions. Every graph also admits $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\min\{n^{4/3},N+(mn)^{3/5}\})$ rounds. Only $n,N$ are inputs. Within the stated graph classes and identifier ranges, these results answer the polynomial-identifier and average-degree questions of Wu and Chrobak. The unrestricted general-graph cases remain open.

item.title: Matrix Multiplication from Polynomial Packings: A Constructive and Elementary Proof of $ω\le9/4$
item.description: We give a self-contained constructive proof that the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies $ω\le9/4$. This bound was recently claimed by OpenAI~\cite{original} through non-constructive arguments in Strassen's asymptotic spectral framework, counting exact scalar arithmetic operations over the complex numbers. We explicitly construct a Strassen-style matrix multiplication identity and obtain the bound by ordinary block recursion. For every $γ>0$, the resulting algorithm multiplies two $n\times n$ integer matrices using $O(n^{9/4+γ})$ integer arithmetic operations.

item.title: Hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over finite chain rings
item.description: We give a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time algorithm for finding hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ over any effectively presented finite chain ring $R$. We call auxiliary group elements or subgroups used to extract information through oracle queries \emph{probes}. For chain length at least two, elementary abelian socle probes first recover the complete flag modulo the maximal ideal. When the residue field has size $q\ge3$, we reconstruct the flag recursively, lifting rank-one terminal members one digit at a time. The intermediate digits reduce to abelian hidden subgroup problems, while the final digit is a finite-field multiple-shift problem solved using learning from subset and Fourier sampling. For $q=2$, where distinct flags can have the same stabilizer, we instead lift the conjugate parabolic subgroup through the congruence filtration. A final linear system determines it modulo normalizer directions. The algorithm outputs generators with probability at least $1-ε$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log|R|,\log(1/ε))$. Consequences include $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ for every $N\ge2$ and, with an explicit maximal-order presentation, $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O_K}/N\mathcal{O_K})$ for number fields $K$.

item.title: Lower Bounds for Minimal-Transversal Enumeration of Bounded-Dimension Hypergraphs and the maximum Minimal Hitting Set Problem
item.description: We present lower bounds for the maximum minimal hitting set problem and for the problem of enumeration of minimal transversals in bounded-dimension hypergraphs. Our starting point is the recent reduction of Kobayashi, Kurita, and Wasa (2026), developed to establish ETH-based hardness of hypergraph dualization. Adapting their construction, we show that, under ETH, deciding whether a hypergraph $\mathcal{G}$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ hyperedges has a minimal transversal of size at least $k$ cannot be done in time $n^{f(k)}m^{o(k)}$, for an arbitrary computable $f$. We transfer this bound to the following decision problem: given a dimension-at-most-$r$ hypergraph and a family of $s$ of its minimal transversals, decide whether another exists. Under ETH, this problem admits no uniform algorithm with running time $n^{f(r)}(s+1)^{o(r)}$. Under SETH, for every fixed $t \geq 2$, it admits no algorithm with running time $\poly(|\mathcal{G}|)(s+1)^c$ for dimension at most $2t$ and any $c<t$. As corollaries, the same exponent obstructions hold for the total time of any output-polynomial enumeration algorithm, with $s$ replaced by the total number of minimal transversals. In particular, polynomial delay is excluded under SETH already for dimension at most four.

item.title: A 55-Addition Rank-23 Scheme for $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication via Exact Two-Sided Minimization
item.description: We give a scheme that multiplies two $3\times3$ matrices with 23 multiplications and 55 additions over any ring, one addition below the previous record of 56 (Sun, 2026) and the first below 56 for exact non-commutative $3\times3$ multiplication without a change of basis. The scheme forms 13 signed combinations of the entries of A and 14 of B, takes 23 products, and recombines them with 28 further additions; its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4. The previous records, from 60 down to 56, were obtained by greedy common-subexpression elimination, which only bounds each side of a scheme from above. We minimize both input sides exactly by chain covering, and the output side exactly through the transposition principle: the 9-by-23 output map costs its transpose plus 14, and the transpose is a 9-input map that the input-side minimizer solves exactly. Applied to Perminov's cn122 scheme (class i19w225c4efh, published at 58 additions) this gives 55 = 13 + 14 + 28, where greedy elimination reaches only 29 on the output side. The same method shows that Sun's representative is output-optimal at 56, and an exact orbit-wide computation over the Heule-Kauers-Seidl database shows that the record class is the only database class attaining 55.

item.title: Simple Strategy-Iteration with Dantzig's Rule is not Strongly Polynomial on Turn-Based Deterministic Games
item.description: We study turn-based deterministic zero-sum games with discounted and long-run average costs. For discounted costs, we establish exponential and superpolynomial iteration lower bounds for the simple strategy-iteration method with Dantzig's rule under unrestricted costs and unit weights, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this shows for the first time that the method is not strongly polynomial even when all action costs belong to $\{-1,0,1\}$. For long-run average costs, we establish an exponential iteration lower bound for termination of a Dantzig counterpart with unrestricted costs and prove that it admits a strongly polynomial implementation with unit weights.

item.title: On the Support Geometry and Complexity of LABS
item.description: LABS are a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem arising in sequence design and statistical physics, yet the formal complexity of the standard fixed-geometry problem remains unresolved. We study how zero-energy complexity changes when support geometry is included as part of the input and then progressively restricted. For unary standard LABS, we establish membership in $\NP$ and a sparsity/Mahaney consequence: Karp NP-hardness would imply $\Ptime=\NP$. For Pair-Set-LABS and Masked-LABS, zero-energy feasibility is polynomial-time decidable when every pair group or masked row has at most three terms and is NP-complete when four terms are allowed. NP-completeness persists when active supports are restricted to contiguous intervals.

item.title: Small sums of roots of unity: polylogarithmic exceptional sets and conditional separation
item.description: We prove a polylogarithmic exceptional-set estimate for symmetric five-term sums of roots of unity of arbitrary order. More precisely, at most $O((\log(2N))^{11})$ points of the $N$-grid satisfy $|1+2\cos(2πx)+2\cos(2πy)|<\exp(-C(\log(2N))^{13})$. This implies the corresponding bound for small conjugates at the reduced conductor: outside polylogarithmically many real embeddings, every such sum is at least quasipolynomially large. The proof is unconditional and combines a polynomial-vector-field multiplicity estimate, arithmetic jet determinants, analytic propagation, and interpolation determinants for nearby grid points. As a companion result, assuming a uniform number-field $abc$ conjecture, we prove that every sum of a fixed number of distinct prime-order roots of unity has modulus at least $\exp(-\varepsilon p)$ for every $\varepsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large primes $p$, uniformly in the exponents. That proof uses simultaneous compression of the exponents, discriminant estimates, and cyclic resultants.

item.title: A Short Note on Algorithms For The Noisy $k$-XOR Problem
item.description: This mostly expository note studies the sample-noise regimes in which the testing problem for noisy $k$-XOR in dimension $n$ can be efficiently solved. Concretely, we ask what pairs $(β, δ)$ admit algorithms running in time $n^{O(k)}$ where $m = n^β, β\in [0,k]$ is the number of samples and $\mathsf{Bern}(n^{-δ}),δ\in (0,+\infty)$ is the noise distribution. The current state-of-the-art algorithms are: I. A folklore algorithm when $β> 1, δ>1$ based on Gaussian elimination; II. A folklore algorithm when $β\ge k/2$ based on the birthday paradox; III. A recent algorithm in the regime $β> δ+ k(1-δ), δ\in (0,1)$ based on a reduction to the first algorithm [DJ24,CSZ24]. IV. Extending [AF09], we strictly improve the last regime to $β> δ+ (k-1)(1-δ), δ\in (0,1).$ These algorithms correspond to efficiently finding short cycles in uniform hypergraphs and can be equivalently phrased as algorithmic Moore bounds.

item.title: Partitionability is NP-complete
item.description: We show that the problem of deciding whether a simplicial complex is partitionable is NP-complete in dimensions two and higher, answering a 1995 question of Kleinschmidt and Onn.

item.title: Bidirectionality is Necessary in Cellular Machines for Exact-Arrival Multi-Agent Path Finding
item.description: On ranked directed acyclic graphs coupled by vertex conflicts we study exact-arrival multi-agent path finding (departure and arrival pinned in place and time) posed as a distributed output task: every cell must emit its own bit of a valid joint path-support mask. The machines are cellular: one automaton per cell, state factored over cells, communication only along a fixed local fabric, synchronous rounds, a query-independent output round, no central decoder, and a per-topology transition code. "Necessary" here means: on an explicit hard topology, over all its feasible queries, no universally correct local-only architecture can renounce either temporal orientation; with global flags, impossibility becomes a bandwidth-round trade-off. The class is not vacuous: a flooding machine solves every instance in as many rounds as the diameter of the local fabric. The bound survives two concessions: we supply every agent's exact individual cavity, which alone solves the single-agent problem in zero rounds and makes the single-agent direction theorem vacuous; and we allow $k$ one-bit global aggregate flags. On a twelve-cell, two-agent, depth-three topology no forward-only machine with $k=0$ is correct on two feasible queries, for any number of rounds; the time-reversed topology does the same to backward-only machines. Placing $p$ copies side by side gives, for forward-only machines, $J_R+kR\ge p$ at constant depth, where $J_R$ measures how much of the query reaches the targets' cones and is $0$ here. A backward-only machine solves that family in constant rounds and a flag-streaming one in $\lceil p/k\rceil+O(1)$, so the bound is tight in order; on the composite family neither orientation can be renounced. The finite lemmas of the gadget and the pair-invariance contradictions are checked in Lean 4; the semantic bridge, the cone lemma and the counting are paper proofs. We report no benchmarks.

item.title: PSPACE-Completeness of the Reachability Relation of Robust Dynamical Systems
item.description: Dynamical systems are a widely used model of computation and an intuitive representation of many natural phenomena in many applied fields. The last decades have seen an impressive use of computers in studying and analysing them, with several visible theoretical breakthroughs. The question of reachability for dynamical systems is central: given two points, is there a trajectory between them in the dynamical system? Reachability, in particular over the reals, is undecidable in the general case: it is only computably enumerable, even under reasonable hypotheses, e.g. for a computable dynamics in general. But it is known to become decidable, and even lies in PSPACE, under suitably quantified robustness assumptions. In this paper, we focus on PSPACE-completeness results over the reals, in the sense of computable analysis, regarding discrete-time and continuous-time robust dynamical systems. We prove that, under some additional and rather reasonable hypotheses, the reachability relation becomes even PSPACE-complete for both classical and second-order complexity second-order complexity, for an adapted notion of reduction. As a side-effect, we also prove an improvement of an algebraic Ordinary Differential Equations-based characterisation of PSPACE, removing one of the base functions of the algebra. By doing so, we link results from dynamical systems and complexity over the reals, including the models of computable analysis and second-order complexity.

item.title: Approximating Independent Sets Using Additive Combinatorics
item.description: We give a deterministic quasi-polynomial time algorithm for approximating the largest independent set in a graph. We show that if an $N$-vertex graph contains an independent set of size $2^{-t} N$, then we can find an independent set of size $2^t$ in quasi-polynomial time, for all $t$ up to a constant factor of $(\log N)^{1/3}$. This gives an approximation factor of $N / \exp((\log N)^{1/3})$, which has the same shape as known hardness results for quasi-polynomial time algorithms, up to a different exponent of the logarithm. The algorithm builds on a structural principle: a graph containing a large independent set must also contain a large sparse structured set, and such a set can be found efficiently. A greedy algorithm then extracts an independent set from it. Our proof draws on tools in additive combinatorics, in particular spreadness and sifting, to obtain the combinatorial structural results. We then convert these to efficient algorithms using pseudo-marginals obtained by semidefinite programming.

item.title: BQP^cc is not contained in MA^cc
item.description: We exhibit a bipartite language with a poly-logarithmic quantum communication protocol and polynomial Merlin-Arthur communication complexity.

item.title: Improved Space Bounds for Promise Graph Coloring in Adversarial Streams
item.description: We study promise graph coloring in one pass insertion-only adversarial streams. We give a randomized algorithm that distinguishes 3-colorable graphs from graphs that are not 6-colorable using $O(n^{3/2}\log(n/\varepsilon)\log n)$ bits of space. This provides a truly subquadratic space algorithm for a constant coloring gap, answering an open problem posed by Assadi, Sundaresan, and Yazdanyar [SODA 2026] for $q=3$. Combining this algorithm with the vertex-sampling lemma of Assadi et al.\ yields, for any $144\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\le Q\le n$, a one-pass decision algorithm distinguishing $3$-colorable graphs from graphs that are not $Q$-colorable using $O((n/Q)^{3/2}\log^5 n)$ bits of space. This improves upon the $\widetilde{O}((n/Q)^2)$ bound achievable via dynamic streaming techniques. Setting $Q=\lceil n^{1/3}\rceil$ yields a semi-streaming decision algorithm, answering the decision version of another open problem posed by Assadi et al. On the negative side, we prove that distinguishing $χ(G)\le q$ from $χ(G)\ge(q-1)^2$ requires $Ω(n^2/q^5)$ bits of space, improving upon the previously established $q^2/4$ threshold using the same space complexity.

item.title: Electrostatic Limits on Quantum Spatial Search
item.description: We prove that a quantum walker cannot search a two-dimensional lattice in Grover's $O(\sqrt N)$ time, resolving the long-standing open question posed by Aaronson and Ambainis in 2003. A walker that hops between neighbouring sites of an $L\times L$ lattice, $N=L^2$, needs $Ω(\sqrt{N\log N})$ local steps at least to find a marked vertex, even with unlimited memory and free queries. Hence, Tulsi's algorithm is asymptotically optimal. Our proof rests on a surprising correspondence with classical electrostatics. We treat the marked vertex as a point charge and weight the overlap between the walker's states with and without the mark by the potential drop, which vanishes where queries act. Only local steps change this weighted overlap, at a rate limited by the field energy, so the lower bound is set by the self-potential of the charge. In the plane this self-potential grows logarithmically with system size, like the Coulomb potential, leading to the extra root-logarithmic factor. Several marked vertices turn the charge into a conductor, and the lower bound depends on their arrangement through its capacitance.

item.title: Unconditional Quantum PAC Learning Advantage in the Large Error Regime
item.description: We establish an unconditional super-polynomial separation between quantum and classical PAC learning of Boolean functions under the uniform distribution in the large error regime. For every advantage $λ(n) = n^{-ω(1)}$, we construct a concept class that a polynomial-time quantum learner learns to agreement $1/2+λ(n)$ with success probability at least $1-1/n^k$. The learner uses only quantum random examples and outputs a polynomial-size deterministic classical circuit. In contrast, no polynomial-time classical learner achieves agreement $1/2 + λ(n)/n^k$ with success probability greater than $1/n^k$, even with membership queries. To achieve this, we develop a nearly-optimal quantum learner that uses quantum random examples to produce a hypothesis achieving a prescribed correlation with an arbitrary Boolean function. The learner generalizes Fourier sampling from parity hypotheses to quadratic hypotheses. While standard Fourier sampling is insensitive to the sign of the correlation, we use interference to bias sampling toward positively correlated hypotheses. This is combined with a careful analysis of the resulting distribution to boost both the learner's success probability and its agreement with the target function. We believe that the resulting quantum learning algorithm might be of independent interest. Finally, although a robust quantum PAC learning advantage holds unconditionally in the large error regime, we note that an analogous separation between quantum and classical learning in the small error regime would imply that $\mathsf{NP} \nsubseteq \mathsf{BPP}$.

item.title: Concrete Functions in Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages and Structural Limitations
item.description: Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on $n$-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' $n$-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication $(1.633\ldots)n$ qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least $3n$ qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication $3\log_2 3$. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every $k\geq 3$, we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for $k$-bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most $k$ per player, and hence at most $k\log_2 k$ qubits in total.

item.title: An Optimal Gap-Majority Lemma for Bounded Rounds Communication
item.description: Recent work of Sawettamalya and Yu (FOCS 2026) initiated the study of \emph{gap-majority} composition in randomized communication. They showed that if computing a $\{\pm 1\}$-valued function $f$ in $r$ rounds requires $I$ bits of information, then distinguishing $\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i,Y_i)\geq 0.01\sqrt{n}$ from $\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i,Y_i)\leq -0.01\sqrt{n}$ in $r$ rounds requires $n \cdot (I-O(\log n))$ bits of information. They also conjectured that the $O(\log n)$-additive ``loss'' can be further reduced to $O(1)$. In this note, we record that a minor adaptation to their approach combining with a finer analysis achieves the conjectured $O(1)$ loss, establishing a gap-majority lemma for bounded-round communication that is optimal up to constant factors.

item.title: Discrete Temporal CSPs et al
item.description: We revisit the complexity classification of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) for first-order reducts of $(\mathbb{Z},<)$, established by Bodirsky, Martin, and Mottet in 2018. Following their approach, we give a self-contained proof of this classification, correcting several errors in the argument. We further show that, with the exception of cases arising from finite-domain CSPs, all tractable cases are solved by a well-known uniform algorithm, eliminating the need for the collection of ad-hoc algorithms used in the original paper. A central component of the proof allows the analysis to be restricted to first-order reducts of $(\mathbb{Z},<)$ that contain the successor relation. We substantially simplify this reduction and generalize the underlying construction. This generalization allows us to apply the same technique to first-order reducts of the triangular lattice graph and of infinite regular trees, yielding a complete complexity classification for these classes of structures, in particular a $\mathsf{P}$ versus $\mathsf{NP}$-complete dichotomy.

item.title: Strong NP-Hardness of Rank-2 Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
item.description: Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) approximates a nonnegative matrix by the product of two nonnegative matrices with a prescribed inner dimension~$r$. The existence of an exact NMF can be decided in polynomial time for every fixed~$r$, and a best rank-$1$ NMF in the Frobenius norm can be obtained from a truncated singular value decomposition. We prove that computing a best rank-$2$ NMF in the Frobenius norm is strongly NP-hard. Our proof uses a polynomial-time reduction from \textsc{Clique} that produces symmetric positive-definite, completely positive matrices with polynomially bounded integer entries. The same reduction also establishes strong NP-hardness of rank-$2$ symmetric NMF.

item.title: The Six-Dimensional Tarski Problem is $Ω(\log^3 n)$-Hard
item.description: We study the deterministic query complexity of finding a fixed point of a monotone function $f:[n]^d\to[n]^d$, where querying $x$ returns $f(x)$. For fixed $d\ge2$, earlier work established a lower bound of $Ω((\log n)^2)$ and an upper bound of $O_d((\log n)^{\lceil(d+2)/3\rceil})$ for the query complexity. Very recently, several papers obtained improved lower bounds using AI-assisted proofs. In this paper, we further improve these lower bounds to $\text{Tarski}(n,d)=Ω_d((\log n)^{2+\lfloor\log_3(d/2)\rfloor})$. In particular, we obtain the optimal $Θ((\log n)^3)$ deterministic query complexity in six dimensions.

item.title: Parallel Repetition for Entangled Games via Conditional Relative Entropy
item.description: We give a proof of the cubic parallel-repetition bound for finite two-player entangled games using quantum conditional relative entropy. For a game with entangled value $1-\varepsilon<1$ and answer alphabets $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$, its $n$-fold repeated value is at most \[ \exp[-Ω(\varepsilon^3n/L)],\qquad L:=\max\{1,\log(|\mathcal A||\mathcal B|)\}, \] for every $n\ge1$. This recovers Song's cubic rate. We also prove a threshold bound: the probability of winning a fraction at least $1-\varepsilon+δ$ is at most $\exp[-Ω(δ^5n/(\varepsilon^2L))]$ for $0<δ\le\varepsilon$. Our information charge is the decrease in relative entropy when a question reference is discarded. Our comparison states preserve the original conditional question law. A chain rule bounds the coordinate charges using the cost of conditioning on checked wins and retaining checked answers. Our main lemma converts small charges into nearby pure-state descriptions and local corrections, each depending only on one player's question. Together with Song's sampler, these enable approximate local preparation of the conditioned workspace.

item.title: Metric Dimension is NP-complete on Graphs of Treewidth Two
item.description: The metric dimension of a connected graph is the least number of vertices whose distance vectors distinguish all vertices. We show that deciding whether the metric dimension of a graph is at most a given integer is NP-complete on graphs of treewidth at most two. As the problem is polynomial on trees, the graphs of treewidth one, this settles the treewidth threshold of its hardness, which was known to lie between two and twenty-four. The reduction is from satisfiability of formulas in which every literal occurs at most twice. To such a formula with $n$ clauses and $r$ variables it associates a graph $G_\varphi$ of treewidth at most two with $O((n+r)^2)$ vertices, whose metric dimension is $2(n+r)+5$ if the formula is satisfiable and $2(n+r)+6$ otherwise.

item.title: Full AFLs Closed under Nested Iterated $k$-Variate Substitution and Depth-k Storage Automata
item.description: Greibach and Ginsburg (1969) studied abstract families of languages or AFLs. A full AFL is a class of languages closed under the following operations: homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, intersection with regular languages, union, concatenation, and Kleene star. Greibach (1970) used a restricted substitution, called nested iterated substitution, to introduce the notion of super AFLs, which are full AFLs that are further closed under nested iterated substitution. The smallest super AFL was shown to be the class of all context-free languages. From this fact, we focus on Greibach's limited, univariable application of nested iterated substitution and further generalize it into k-variate. This introduces the notion of nested iterated $k$-variate substitution whose definition does not rely on "machines". Recently, a "two-tape" version of Hibbard's (1967) rewriting systems, which were later reformulated by Pighizzini and Pisoni (2014) as k-limited automata with "single" input/work tapes, has been studied under the name of depth-k storage automata. This work unearths a few characteristics of the languages recognized by those automata under a restriction known as frozen blank sensitivity in terms of full AFLs and nested iterated k-variate substitution. This will promote a further abstract treatment of those languages.

item.title: Semi-Linearity and Generalized Stratified Semi-Linearity beyond Context-Free Languages
item.description: Parikh's famous theorem relates to the semi-linearity of context-free languages. We seek for expanding the scope of the semi-linear property from context-free languages to languages beyond them. Of those languages, this work focuses on the languages that are particularly recognized by one-way nondeterministic depth-k storage automata under a natural restriction of frozen blank sensitivity. Those languages (which are called $k$-storable languages) have been already proven to satisfy a natural generalization of the well-known pumping lemmas for regular and context-free languages. The semi-linearity of k-storable languages generalizes Parikh's theorem on the semi-linearity of context-free languages. As for bounded languages, Ginsburg and Spanier's well-known theorem characterizes context-free languages in terms of stratified semi-linearity. This notion is further generalized and is used to characterize the k-storable languages as well. Such a generalization is interesting in its own right. This helps us take an abstract treatment of k-storable languages without relying on "machines". Our results strengthen the belief that those languages are "natural" generalizations of context-free languages.

item.title: The Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-Complete
item.description: Poset games form a fundamental class of combinatorial games that includes classical games such as Nim and Chomp. Determining the outcome of a poset game is known to be PSPACE-complete even for posets of height at most three. However, the exact computational complexity of Two-Level Poset Game, played on posets of height at most two, has remained an open problem for over a decade. We resolve this problem by proving that Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-complete via a polynomial-time reduction from Avoid True on positive CNF formulas.

item.title: Generalized Fibonacci gates are Frobenius algebras: a proof of Liu's conjecture
item.description: Liu introduced generalized Fibonacci gates on domains of size 3 and 4, proved that Holant problems built from them are tractable by a cut-and-merge algorithm, and conjectured that Fibonacci gates with matching polynomial-time algorithms exist on all higher domains. We extend the definition uniformly to every domain size $k$ and show that a family of domain-$k$ generalized Fibonacci gates is the same thing as a $k$-dimensional commutative Frobenius (equivalently, Artinian Gorenstein) algebra $A$ equipped with an orthonormal basis containing $1$. Under this dictionary Liu's parameter constraints are exactly associativity of $A$, a gate is an element $w\in A$, merging two gates is multiplication in $A$, and the Holant value of a connected graph $G$ is $τ\bigl(h^{\,|E|-|V|+1}\prod_v w_v\bigr)$ for a fixed ``handle'' element $h\in A$. This proves Liu's conjecture for every $k$, with an algorithm whose cost is polynomial in $k$ as well as in the graph. We also give a closure criterion for linear recurrences of any depth (a balance condition implies closure, and is necessary when the unit is a combination of the colours), and we map the landscape: semisimple algebras are exactly Liu's orthogonal frames, smoothable algebras with nilpotents are collided frames, and families whose algebra is not smoothable (``frameless'' families) exist exactly when $k\ge 14$. Finally we show that every non-semisimple part of a family is invisible to the Holant on connected graphs with two or more independent cycles. This note states the results and sketches the proofs; the proofs of the main theorems are short and are given essentially in full.

item.title: Majority and Torus Polynomials: Bounded-Lift Lower Bounds and Explicit Constructions
item.description: Bhrushundi et al. (2019) introduced torus polynomial approximation as an approach to separating Majority from $ACC^0$. In this model, approximation is measured modulo integers. Krishan and Vishwanathan (2026) developed a duality framework for lower bounds and posed five open problems. We resolve two of these, concerning integer lifts and explicit polynomial approximations. An integer lift records the integer shifts that turn a torus approximation into an ordinary real approximation. We show that a degree-d torus polynomial approximating Majority with error at most 1/8 and lift contained in an interval of width $B$ must satisfy $d(B + 1) = Ω(n)$. This rules out low-degree approximating polynomials with lifts in {-1, 0, 1}, answering their Open Problem 2. We also answer Open Problem 5 by giving, for every Boolean function on $n \geq 1$ variables, an explicit torus polynomial approximation of degree at most $n - 1$. Its error is optimal: zero when the accepting set has even cardinality and $2^{-n-1}$ otherwise. The results presented were discovered and formalized in Lean using GPT-6 Astra.

item.title: Nearly Optimal Quantum Sample Complexity of Learning Fourier-Sparse Boolean Functions
item.description: We study the number of uniform quantum examples needed to exactly learn a Boolean function with at most $k$ nonzero Fourier coefficients. We give a learner with near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(k)$ sample complexity independent of the input length $n$. The learner uses only separate measurements of individual examples. This improves the previous $O(k^{3/2}\log^2 k)$ upper bound (Arunachalam, Chakraborty, Lee, Paraashar, and de Wolf, 2021). The main ingredient is a candidate set formed by symmetric differences of subsets from independent groups of Fourier samples. A multilinear majority polynomial combines unbiased random approximations into an accurate witness whose Fourier support lies in this set. Granularity then forces the set to contain the entire Fourier support, including subsets never directly sampled. For comparison, we derive the tight classical sample complexity $Θ(nk)$ by combining known sparse-recovery and lower-bound results.

item.title: Polynomial Separation of a Shared Tensor Leg and Matrix Multiplication in Arbitrary Characteristic
item.description: We improve the shared-leg separation construction in Proposition 3.1 of OpenAI, *An Upper Bound of $9/4$ for the Matrix Multiplication Exponent* (October 2, 2026). If $M$ tensor blocks have a common first space and independent matched sectors on their other two spaces, then $M+n-1$ copies of their matched sum degenerate to the full direct sum of the blocks, each tensored with an $n$-dimensional dot product. For $n=M$, this reduces the number of source copies from $5M$ to $2M-1$. The construction uses polynomial interpolation and truncated local substitution, with no roots of unity or factorial denominators. It works over every field containing enough distinct elements. We verify that the remaining spectral and discrete-growth arguments of the cited preprint are independent of characteristic. Over an algebraic closure, the replacement therefore gives $ω\leq9/4$ in every characteristic.

item.title: Superpolynomial Lists for Reed-Solomon Codes over Binary Extension Fields
item.description: Recent work shows that ordinary Reed--Solomon codes over prime fields admit polynomial-size lists up to list-decoding capacity on every evaluation set. We show a contrasting phenomenon over binary extension fields. For every fixed rate $0<R<1$, there exists $\varepsilon_R>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $h$, the full-field Reed--Solomon code over $\mathbb{F}_{2^h}$ has a received word with $n^{Ω_R(\log n)}$ codewords within relative distance $1-R-\varepsilon_R$. To our knowledge, these are the first superpolynomial ordinary Reed--Solomon list-size lower bounds at fixed positive rate and a fixed positive agreement gap above the rate. Thus capacity-approaching polynomial list size for Reed--Solomon codes is not uniform over the underlying field, and the obstruction occurs at every fixed rate.
